name: Assir
title: Son of Korah, a Levite from the family of Kohath
summary: Assir was a Levite of the family of Kohath and a son of Korah. His father led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, and the rebels met God’s judgment when the earth opened up and fire consumed them. Yet Korah’s sons survived (Num 26:11), and Assir, together with his brothers Elkanah and Abiasaph, became an ancestor of the family of the Korahites. This family was given prominent duties connected to the sanctuary. In later generations their descendants served as singers and gatekeepers at the tabernacle and temple, under the service order established by King David. The spiritual legacy of Korah’s sons is especially visible through the psalms that bear their names—psalms marked by deep longing for God, praise, and trust in Him.

keyEvents.description: Several psalms are attributed to Korah's sons, testifying to the rich spiritual heritage of this family and their deep longing for God and praise.

versions.summary: Assir was a son of Korah, who was a Levite from the line of Kohath. Although his father Korah led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron and was punished by God, Korah's descendants survived and became important servants in the temple. Korah's sons, including Assir, became ancestors of a Levitical family that later played a significant role in temple music.
versions.title: Descendant of Korah
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Descendant of Korah' is slightly imprecise – Assir was a son of Korah, not merely a descendant. 'Son of Korah' is more accurate.; [major] Assir is not described as a priest in the Bible. He was a Levite, not a priest. Levites and priests held different roles. The descendants of Korah served as singers and gatekeepers, not as priests. The role should be changed to 'Levite'.; [major] In Exodus 6:24, Korah's sons are listed as Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. However, in 1 Chronicles 6:22-23 (Hebrew numbering may vary), it appears that Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph might be part of a linear genealogy rather than siblings. Regardless, according to Exodus 6:24 they are brothers, so this is acceptable. However, the IDs should be verified – 'elkana' and 'abiasaf' should be checked for correctness.; [critical] The reference is given as Exodus 6:24 (bookId 2, chapter 6, verse 24), which is correct – this is where Assir is mentioned as a son of Korah. This is accurate.; [minor] 1 Chronicles 6:22-23,37 – the verse numbering in 1 Chronicles chapter 6 can vary between different translations (Hebrew versus others). In some translations, Assir is mentioned in verse 22, in others in verse 37. It is important to be aware of this, but the references are reasonable.; [minor] The summary mentions 'the temple', but during Assir's time the temple did not yet exist. It was first built under Solomon. This should be phrased more precisely, for example as 'the tabernacle' or by noting that his descendants later served in the temple.; [minor] 'Exodus' is appropriate for Assir, who lived during the wilderness wanderings. The lifespan 'around 1400 BC' is also reasonable given traditional chronology.

His father Korah led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron and was punished by God, but Korah's sons survived (Num 26:11). Assir and his brothers Elkanah and Abiasaph became ancestors of a Levitical family that later played an important role in service at the tabernacle and later in the temple, especially in music and gatekeeping. The spiritual heritage of the Korahites is attested through several psalms attributed to Korah's sons.
versions.title: Son of Korah, a Levite from the family of Kohath
versions.reason: [major] The verse references in 1 Chronicles 6 vary between Hebrew and Greek/Western numbering. In the Hebrew text, Assir is mentioned in 1 Chron 6:7-8 (which corresponds to 6:22-23 in many translations). Verse 37 of 1 Chron 6 refers to a different context. It is safer to refer to the verses that actually mention Assir directly. In many translations, it is 1 Chron 6:22 and 6:37 that are relevant, but verse 23 mentions Elkanah, not Assir directly. Should be adjusted for precision.; [minor] Assir was not just a Levite in general, but specifically belonged to the clan of Kohath. The role 'ancestor of the Korahite lineage' could have been included to provide a more complete picture.; [minor] The summary is good, but resembles version 1 very closely. It should be rephrased more clearly to differentiate itself from the earlier version and provide even greater independent value.; [minor] 1 Chron 6:31-33 deals with David's general arrangement of singers, but does not directly link Assir. It is 1 Chron 6:33-38 (depending on the version) that gives the genealogical line back to Korah through Assir. Consider including verses that more clearly connect Assir's lineage to the singing service.; [minor] The connection between the name 'prisoner' and the earth's gap is an interesting observation, but it is speculative. It should be clarified that this is an interpretive link, not an established etymological relationship.

versions.summary: Assir was a Levite of the family of Kohath and a son of Korah. His father led a well-known rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, where the rebels were swallowed up by the earth as God's judgment. Yet Korah's sons escaped (Num 26:11). Assir and his brothers Elkanah and Abiasaf thus became ancestors of the family of the Korahites, who received prominent duties connected with the sanctuary. In later generations their descendants served as singers and gatekeepers at the tabernacle and in the temple. The spiritual legacy of Korah's sons is especially visible through the psalms that bear their names—psalms marked by deep longing for God and praise.
versions.title: Son of Korah, a Levite from the family of Kohath
versions.reason: [major] The verse references in 1 Chr 6 are problematic. In the Hebrew text (MT), 1 Chr 6 has a different verse numbering than many translations. Verse 22 in some translations corresponds to verse 7 in the MT, and verse 37 can refer to different people depending on the numbering. Assir is mentioned in 1 Chr 6:22-23 (some translations 6:37), but one should verify the exact verse numbering. The footnotes themselves mention this problem, but the references should still be as precise as possible.; [minor] Verses 31-33 and 37-38 in 1 Chr 6 concern David's singers and their lineage, but it is worth checking that verses 37-38 actually mention Assir's lineage specifically, since verse numbering varies between textual traditions.; [minor] The summary is good and clearly different from earlier versions. One small clarification: the phrasing 'swallowed by the earth' is correct for Dathan and Abiram (Num 16:31-33), while Korah's 250 men were consumed by fire (Num 16:35). There is some ambiguity in the text about whether Korah himself was swallowed by the earth or consumed by fire. A nuance would strengthen the theological precision.; [minor] The ID 'elkana' for Assir's brother could potentially be confused with other biblical figures named Elkana (e.g., Samuel's father). Ensure that the ID points to the correct person in the database. If disambiguation exists (e.g., 'elkana-korah-son'), it should be used.; [minor] The role 'ancestor of the Korahite lineage' is good. One could also consider adding something like 'mentioned in the Levitical genealogy' to emphasize his function in the genealogical lists, but this is not strictly necessary.

footnotes.text: The name Assir (Hebrew: אַסִּיר, 'Assir') can mean 'captive' or 'bound'. This meaning of the name has been noted by several commentators, although there is no certain connection between the meaning of the name and his father's fate. In ancient Israel, names often carried a prophetic or circumstantial significance.

The survival of Korah's sons (Num 26:11) constitutes an important theological point in the biblical narrative: God's judgment is just and individual. This idea is expanded in Ezek 18:20, where it is stated that a son shall not bear his father's guilt. The continued service of the Korahites shows that grace and restoration are possible even after serious sin within a family.

Several psalms (Ps 42, 44–49, 84–85, 87–88) are attributed to 'the sons of Korah' in their headings. This collection contains some of the most poetic and theologically rich texts in the Book of Psalms, including Psalm 42 about the soul's longing for God and Psalm 84 about the joy of being in God's presence.

According to 1 Chron 6:31-48, David organized the musical service of the Levites at the sanctuary. Heman, one of the three chief singers, was according to the genealogy a descendant of Korah. This line went through Asaph and continued down through the generations.

Temple singers and gatekeepers were important offices throughout the ancient Near East. Texts from Mesopotamia and Egypt testify to similar cultic music traditions, placing the biblical Levitical musical service in a broader cultural context.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles chapter 6 have different verse numbering in various textual traditions. The Hebrew Bible (Masoretic Text) and different translations can differ by up to 15 verses in their numbering. This makes it important to check the context when looking up references in this chapter.

In rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Sanhedrin 110a), the survival of Korah's sons is discussed. One tradition tells that they repented in their hearts as the earth opened, and that they were preserved on a ledge in the abyss. This underscores the rabbinic emphasis on the power of repentance, even at the last moment.
